To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
breastmilk viral load was high in women with subclinical mastititis and severe maternal immune suppression.

breast milk HIV RNA viral loads were high in the first 6 weeks after birth, were associated with sub-clinical mastitis and maternal immunodeficiency and that the mode of infant feeding did not influence viral loads.
the viral load of breastmilk in the first 6 months of life varies and is associated with subclinical breast inflammation, and with maternal HIV disease severity.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of subclinical breastmilk mastitis on HIV transmission.
the role of breast milk in the transmission of HIV from mother to child and the factors which may influence the viral load in breast milk and the risk of HIV transmission through breast milk.
the effects of subclinical breast inflammation on breastmilk HIV RNA viral load.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the milk viral load is not a good predictor of transmission.
the viral load of breast milk is a complex variable, and that it is not possible to state conclusively whether breast milk is the main source of HIV transmission to the infant.
breast milk HIV RNA viral levels vary, but are associated with maternal immune status, subclinical mastitis, and infant feeding practices.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

breast milk RNA viral load in South African women was high at 1 and 6 weeks postpartum and was associated with low maternal CD4 cell count and subclinical mastititis, but not with infant feeding mode.

breast milk HIV RNA viral loads were high in the majority of samples, with a significant association between high milk viral load and subclinical mastisitis, low maternal CD4 count, and high infant HIV infection rates.
breast milk HIV RNA viral levels in the first 6 months after birth are not associated with feeding mode.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there was a non-significantly trend for the six HIV-infected infants, compared with the uninfected infants, to have been fed breastmilk of high RNA viral load.
there are a variety of factors that contribute to viral load in breastmilk, and it is difficult to predict viral load in breast milk from maternal factors.
the viral load of the breast milk of HIV-positive women varies greatly, and that the viral load in breast milk is higher in women who have subclinical mastitis or low CD4 counts.
